title: 4 haunted places in Mumbai with paranormal ghost stories people still swear are true
excerpt: From abandoned mills to old chawls, these four allegedly haunted places in Mumbai have a reputation for the eerie and paranormal.
content:
Nothing empty is ever left alone too long in Mumbai. Old buildings and hotels are promptly redeveloped, not leaving much opportunity for hauntings to really set in. And yet, the spooky ‘lady in white’ stories persist.

Over the years, certain corners of Bombay have acquired reputations for being haunted. The stories are often impossible to verify, passed down through local lore and repeated in blog posts and late-night conversations. These allegedly haunted places in Mumbai are as much a story about the city itself as they are about the supernatural.

Aarey Colony

Aarey is one of the more unusual settings for a Mumbai ghost story because the landscape itself is at the centre of the tale.

This colony is a large green area in Goregaon and has long been associated with stories of apparitions appearing on its roads after dark. One of the most repeated versions is about a woman in a white sari, sometimes described as carrying a child, who is said to appear to motorists and ask for a lift. Other versions involve a child or an unexplained figure appearing on the roadside.

Aarey is a large, heavily wooded part of Mumbai, and its roads have long felt removed from the city's more densely built neighbourhoods. The area is also home to wildlife, including leopards, and has experienced real concerns around road safety and movement after dark. The boundary between the city and the forest is unusually close here.

That physical landscape has inevitably shaped the folklore.

In 2025, Hindustan Times quoted Mumbai heritage-walk organiser Bharat Gothoskar discussing Aarey alongside Mukesh Mills and the SNDT campus as places in the city that are said to be haunted. His observation was less about proving the stories than about the way they develop: something happens, a story is told, and eventually the story becomes attached to the landscape.

Mukesh Mills

Mukesh Mills is probably the most recognisable of Mumbai's allegedly haunted locations. It is a former textile mill that sits close to the sea in Colaba, and its industrial buildings have an atmosphere that has made them a favourite location for filmmakers for decades. The mill was established in the late nineteenth or early twentieth century and eventually fell into disuse. A fire in 1982 killed several mill workers, and the property later became known for its film shoots. It closed as a regular film-shooting location in 2019 after concerns were raised about its structural condition. The ghost stories grew alongside its reputation in the film industry.

Bipasha Basu has also described an unsettling experience while filming at Mukesh Mills. In interviews with Rediff and Filmfare, she recalled repeatedly forgetting a monologue she knew by heart while shooting Gunaah at the mill. She said the crew eventually called in a baba and performed a religious ritual at the location before the scene was completed elsewhere. These are Basu’s recollections of the experience, rather than evidence of anything supernatural.

Other actors have told similar stories over the years. Some accounts involve strange noises or a sense of being watched. These are personal recollections rather than evidence of paranormal activity, but their sheer persistence has helped cement Mukesh Mills' reputation.

Sanjay Gandhi National Park

Sanjay Gandhi National Park is a vast protected landscape that exists inside a city otherwise defined by traffic and skyscrapers. Among the supposedly haunted places in Mumbai, it is also the setting for one of the city's most persistent ghost stories.

The recurring tale concerns a woman who is said to appear on roads through the park at night and ask passing motorists for a lift. According to versions of the story repeated by Times of India, park guards have spoken about encounters with a female apparition, while local residents have described strange voices and the sensation of being followed.

Although, it is worth separating this folklore from the park's actual history. Sanjay Gandhi National Park is a living ecosystem. It contains dense vegetation, wildlife and a network of trails and roads, and the city sits immediately outside its boundaries. The park has also been the site of real crimes and accidents over the years. Those events are documented; the ghost story is not.

D’Souza Chawl

D’Souza chawl in Mahim has been repeatedly described in Indian media as one of Mumbai's allegedly haunted places. At the centre of the story is a well.

According to the long-running account, a woman living in the chawl accidentally fell into the well while drawing water and drowned. Residents are said to have subsequently reported seeing a woman around the chawl after dark. In some versions of the story, she is described as a harmless presence who disappears when morning comes.

The story has appeared repeatedly over the years. Times of India has included D'Souza Chawl in more than one feature on India's and Mumbai's allegedly haunted places, while NDTV included it in a 2024 roundup of Mumbai locations said to be haunted. Mid-Day also revisited the story in its 2025 coverage of Mumbai's most popular haunted places.

The strange thing about this one is that D'Souza Chawl is not an abandoned mansion or isolated ruin. It is a lived-in residential community. The ghost story has therefore become part of the lore of an ordinary Mumbai neighbourhood. It is passed around alongside the everyday lives of people in the chawl. That is often how urban folklore survives.

There is a temptation with haunted-place stories to focus on the fright, the figure in the road, the abandoned building, the unexplained sound. But Mumbai's stories are more interesting when they are allowed to sit beside the ordinary history of the places themselves. Mukesh Mills really did burn. D'Souza Chawl really does have a well around which a long-running story has developed. Aarey really is a vast green landscape within an enormous city. Sanjay Gandhi National Park really does contain stretches of forest that can feel far removed from urban Mumbai. The ghost stories have been merged with those realities over time. And in a city that is constantly rebuilding itself, there is something quite compelling about the stories that refuse to move on.
